Medications include intravenous ceftriaxone and ampicil lin, albutero l inhalers, theophy lline, and prednisone. He is confused and stuporous. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows meningismus. An MRI of the brain shows diffuse meningeal enhancement with a basilar predominance. A lumbar puncture is done; cerebrosp inal fluid analysis shows a leukocyte count of 322/mm 3 (86% lymphocytes), a glucose concentration of 17 mg/dL, and a protein concentration of 212 mg/dl. correctExplanation: Chronic use of immunosuppressants including glucocorticoids increase the likelihood of tuberculosis reactivation. However, unlike bacterial meningitis which presents acutely, tuberculous meningitis typica lly shows a subacute presentation. Presence of cranial nerve palsies is also more likely in tuberculous meningitis than bacterial meningitis. Physical examination may show a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign, indicative of meningea l irritation. Results of laboratory studies will show nonspecific changes including leukocytosis and mild anemia. A tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay are usually positive, but a negative result is also possible. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will reveal an increased opening pressure, increased white blood cell count with prominent lymphocytes, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration. Culture of the CSF for acid-fast bacilli may be positive, though the sensitivity of this test for tuberculous meningitis is less than 50%. Radiologic evaluation may show basilar exudates, as in this case, as well as periventricu lar infarcts and hydrocephalus.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by his wife 30 minutes after a 15-minute episode of inability to speak. He has a 15-year history of poorly controlled hypertension . Three weeks ago, he had a transmural myocardial infarction and underwe nt placement of a stent in the left anterior descending coronary artery. Current medications include clopidogrel, benazepril, and 81-mg aspirin. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. On arrival, he is alert and oriented to person , place, and time. His pulse is 60/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. A grade 1 /6 systolic murmur is heard best at the second left intercostal space. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Carotid duplex ultrasonograp hy shows 40% stenosis of the left carotid artery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: An embolic ischemic stroke involves an event in which a clot breaks off and travels to the brain, occluding blood flow within a cerebra l artery. Emboli can originate from proxima l vessels, such as the internal carotid artery, or from an atrial or ventricular thrombus. This patient had a recent myocardial infarction, which predisposes him to a ventricular aneurysm. Ventricular aneurysms are more likely to form in the case of large, anterior myocardia l infarctions as a result of obstruction of the left anterior descending coronary artery, as was the case in this patient. A small systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation may be heard. Within the aneurysm, as a result of areas of stagnant blood flow and despite being on clopidogre l, a thrombus can form that can embolize and cause an ischemic stroke. If a patent foramen ovale is present, an embolism may arise from either the right or left side of the heart. This patient also has other risk factors for ischemic stroke including hypertension and atherosclerotic disease. Because his symptoms resolved within less than 24 hours, his embolic event is classified as a transient ischemic attack.

A lacunar stroke may present with purely motor symptoms, purely sensory symptoms, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria. Infarcts in these deep penetrating vesse ls are secondary to hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hypercholesterolemia. While these risk factors would also predispose to myocardial infarction, this patient's transient ischemic event is most likely caused by an embolism from the left ventricle as opposed to a primary central nervous system infarction. lntraparenchyma l cerebral hemorrhage (Choice C) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Choice E) are both causes of hemorrhagic stroke and are caused by ruptured intracrania l or subarachnoid blood vessels in the setting of hypertension. questionStem: One month after starting isoniazid and rifampin therapy for pulmonary tubercu losis, a 62-year-old woma n develops weakness, fatigue, and paresthesias. Examination shows pallor and diminished light touch sensation in the extremities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in 9 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 78 µm3 Leukocyte count 8000/mm3 Platelet count 210,000 /mm3 These symptoms are most likely to respond to treatment with which of the following?
correctExplanation: lsoniazid and rifampin are used in the treatmen t of primary tuberculosis, which results from an initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. lsoniaz id binds vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) which may result in early excretion and inactivation of pyridoxine, and also inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase, which is necessary to activate it. Pyridoxine deficiency results, of which primary symptoms are peripheral neuropathy and paresthesia. Pyridox ine deficiency limits synthesis of histamine, hemoglobin, and neurotransm itters including epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin, and y-aminobutyric acid (GABA). In addition to peripheral neuropathy, deficiency common ly presents with dermatitis, siderob lastic anemia, glossitis, and seizures. These adverse effects may all be avoided by pyridoxine supplementation in all patients taking isoniazid.

Folate is contained in leafy vegetab les and absorbed in the jejun um. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcoholism, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). It is not caused by isoniazid or rifampin and is not responsible for this patient's symptoms. Iron (Choice B) deficiency also presents with microcytic anemia. questionStem: A 22-year-o ld man who is a collegiate volleyball player comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of progressive pain and weakness in his right shoulder. There is no history of trauma. He is 196 cm (6 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. There is significant loss of muscle mass in the dorsal scapula region, especial ly in the area of the scapular spine. Passive abduction and externa l rotation of the right shoulder and protraction of the scapula reproduce the pain. There is weakness with resisted externa l rotation and initiation of abduction. Active range of motion shows full flexion and abduct ion. Sensory examinat ion shows no cutaneous deficits along the right side of the neck or in the right upper extremity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: The patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are most consistent with entrapment of the suprascapu lar nerve. The suprascapular nerve originates from the superior trunk of the brachia! plexus and innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. Nerve compression secondary to traction injury is common among volleyball players. Irritation of the suprascapular nerve results in pain along the course of the nerve and may result in chronic neuropathy with subsequent muscle wasting, atrophy, and degeneration of the infraspinatus and supraspinatus muscles. The supraspinatus is responsib le for adduction of the shoulder, and the infraspinatus is responsible for external rotation of the shoulder, which reproduce the pain and disclose weakness in this patient. Initial treatment is conservative with activity modification and physical therapy. Operative intervention may be required.

Patients typically note a gradua l onset of progressive shoulder stiffness and pain. Physical examination would disclose limited range of motion while this patient discloses full range of motion. Axillary nerve damage (Choice B) results in weakness of the deltoid and teres minor, which abduct and stabilize the shoulder. The axillary nerve gives rise to the superficial lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, and sensory deficits would be expected if injured. Brachia! plexus palsy (Choice C) describes a range of injury to the nervous system complex that gives rise to the nerves of the upper extremity. The mechanism is usually high-impact trauma or forced abduction of the shoulder. questionStem: A physician makes a house call for an 87-year-old woman who is unable to come to the office because of difficulty with transportat ion. Her family reports that she has fallen frequent ly during the past 6 weeks. The patient says that she has had some difficulty feeling where her feet are but that she is otherwise well. She has not had loss of consciousness. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. Vital signs are within normal limits. Muscle strength is 4/5 on flexion of the hips and extension of the knees and ankles bilaterally. Proprioceptio n and sensation to vibrat ion are decreased in the lower extrem ities. Sensation to light touch is intact. She has a slapping gait. Mental status examination shows no abnorma lities. The physician counsels the patient about making enhancements to her home to prevent falls. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Subacute combined degeneration causes a combination of motor and sensory symptoms including ataxic gait, muscle weakness, paresthesia , and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. The effects of these features may include frequent falls, as in this case. Vitamin B 12 deficiency is often a result of inadequate dietary intake, seen in veganism, malabsorption, or pernicious anemia. Occasiona lly, elderly patients with poor nutrition may develop B 12 deficiency. Other manifestations include dementia and megaloblastic anemia. In an elderly patient with an acute or subacute change in behavior or activities of daily living, organic causes such as vitamin deficiency should be ruled out.

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld nulligravid woman has had cafe au lait spots and multiple neurofibromas since birth. A diagnosis of neurofibromatos is is made. She is concerned that she might pass this condition on to her children. Her parents and three siblings do not have this disorder. The risk for neurofibromatosis in her children is closest to which of the following?

choices.A: 50% for each child , since neurofibromatosis is autosomal dominan t
choices.B: 25% for each child, since neurofibroma tosis is autosoma l recess ive
choices.C: 10% for each child, since neurofibroma tosis is contro lled by severa l genes
choices.D: No risk, since neurofibromatos is is not a genet ic disorder
choices.E: No risk, since the patient represe nts a new mutat ion

correctExplanation: Neurofibromatosis type I is a genetically inherited disorder caused by a defect in NF1, the gene which encodes neurofibromin on chromosome 17. It follows an autosoma l dominant pattern of inheritance. It is characterized by a constellation of cutaneous manifestations (eg, neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, cafe au lait spots, and axillary freckling), a variety of central nervous system tumors including optic nerve glioma and iris hamartoma (ie, Lisch nodu le), and bony abnorma lities such as long bone dysp lasia and sphenoid wing dysplasia. Patients are also at higher risk for developing astrocytomas, brainstem gliomas, and soft tissue sarcomas. Because it follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, only one alle le is needed to develop the condition. Thus, the chance of this patient passing on the dominant allele containing the mutation on chromosome 17 is 50% for each child.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. 25% for each child (Choice B) wou ld be the chance of a child deve loping an autosoma l recessive disease if both his or her parents were carriers. The defect in NF1 that causes neurofibromatosis type I is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. 10% for each child (Choice C) could be the chance of a deve loping a disease which is controlled by several genes, or for which there is variable penetrance or expressivity, but neurofibromatosis type I is caused by a defect in a single gene, NF1, located on chromosome 17. No risk for developing neurofibromatosis (Choice D) is incorrect as the disease is a genetic disorder. Whi le the patient likely does represent a new mutation (Choice E) given that her parents are unaffected, this does not change the patient's risk for passing on her mutation to her children. questionStem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician 2 hours after the sudden onset of visual loss in his right eye. He has no history of similar episodes . He has a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin and hypertension treated with lisinopril. He sustained a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. His pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 170/96 mm Hg. Findings on right funduscopic exam ination are shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting signs and symptoms of abrupt, painless vision loss and a pale fundus with normal fovea l color are consistent with a diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). CRAO commonly occurs as a result of embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery but may occur secondary to vasculitis, such as in giant cell arteritis (GCA). Patients may have a history of preceding amaurosis fugax. Examination shows profound diminishment of visual acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a pale fundus with preserved foveal color. CRAO is a medical emergency, as it an ischemic stroke of the ophthalmic vasculature and indicates a high risk for associated ischemic stroke to the brain. Patients who present with CRAO should be admitted to a stroke center for emergent evaluation, including a search for a possible embolic source with echocardiography and duplex ultrasonography of the carotid arteries. A careful history and laboratory evaluation of erythrocyte sedimentation rate, serum concentration of C-reactive protein, and platelet count should be performed to evaluate for possible GCA. There is no proven medical or surgical therapy for CRAO, and the visual prognosis Is poor.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (Choice A) typically presents with pain, conjunctiva! injection, a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, increased intraocular pressure, and no visible fundus abnormalities. If acute angle-closure glaucoma is not treated promptly it may result in profound, irreversible vision loss. Bacterial conjunctivitis (Choice B) presents with pain, conjunctiva ! injection, and purulent discharge. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of painful burning sensations in her hands and feet. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropr iate initial pharmacotherapy?

choices.E: Topical lidocaine to the affected areas

correctExplanation: Peripheral neuropathy is a frequent finding in patients with HIV and may occur either secondary to direct viral infection of peripheral nerves or secondary to neurotoxicity associated with antiretrovira l medications, frequent ly medications in the nucleoside analog reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) class. HIV-associated neuropathy most frequently presents with symmetric, distal polyneuropathy characterized by sensations of burning, tingling, or numbness in a stocking-g love distribution, as well as reduced vibratory or pinprick sensation. As with other forms of distal polyneuropathy, tricyclic antidepressants such as nortriptyline are effective as first-line treatment. Other effective treatments include gabapentin, pregabalin, lamotrigine, and topical capsaicin or lidocaine.

While some SSRls, such as duloxetine, may be effective for the treatment of neuropathic pain, fluoxetine is not effective in treating nerve pain. Oral lorazepam (Choice B) is a short-acting benzodiazepine and is not recommended for the treatment of neuropathic pain because of its significant adverse effects and risk for dependency. Oral prednisone (Choice D) is a corticosteroid. While corticoste roids, including prednisone, may be effective for some forms of neuropathic pain, this is not an appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient given the significan t adverse effects of corticosteroid s, which includes immunosuppression. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of moderate low back pain. He thinks he may have hurt his back while doing yard work. His pain moderate ly improves with rest; he has been spending a great amount of time in bed. He has not had other symptoms, weight loss, or a recent infection. He has no history of serious illness. His only medication is ibuprofen for the pain. He does not use intravenous drugs or anabolic steroids. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 102 kg (225 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m2. correctExplanation: Low back pain is a common presenting complaint and it can be difficult to identify an exact underlying cause. Most nonspecific low back pain is attributed to muscu loskeletal injury from exertion, overuse, or trauma. The majority of these cases will resolve with conservative management, which includes activity modification, stretching, over-the-counter analgesics such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), massage, acupuncture, and heat therapy. Certain red flag signs and symptoms should prompt more urgent eva luation for a cause, especia lly if there is concern for infection, malignancy, or fracture. These include new fevers, intravenous drug use, focal neurologic deficits (such as urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bowel incontinence which may suggest cauda equina syndrome), progressive lower extremity neurologic symptoms, current or recent cancer history, advanced age, systemic corticosteroid use, and a significant traumatic mechanism. In this young, otherwise healthy patient with a mild inciting event, the next best step in management is continuation of ibuprofen therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bed rest for 10 days (Choice A) is not recommended for acute low back pain, as patients tend to have increased pain and a slower return to normal function. Activity modification for symptom relief should be advised, with encouragement to continue normal activities of daily living and non-exacerbating exertion. X-ray of the lumbar spine (Choice B) and MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice C) should be reserved for patients who present with red flag signs and symptoms to evaluate for evidence of fracture, infection, or malignancy. For otherwise healthy patients with back pain that has persisted for less than 4 weeks, imaging studies do not genera lly change management. Oxycodone therapy as needed for pain (Choice E) should be reserved for severe or refractory cases of acute low back pain. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 10-day-old newbor n is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after a seizure that involved clonic jerking of the left arm. He had been well until 2 days ago when he began sleeping somewhat more but continued to feed well. Pregnancy, labor, and delivery were uncomplica ted. Vital signs are within normal limits. He is difficult to awaken but moves all extremities when stimulated. He is hypotonic but hyperreflexic. Babinski sign is present. During examinat ion, he has a clonic seizure of the right lower extrem ity. A CT scan of the head shows no abnorma lities. Cerebrospina l fluid analysis shows: Glucose Protein Leukocyte count Erythrocyte count A Gram stain is negative . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: 55 mg/dl 110 mg/dl 85/mm3 860/mm 3 Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) encepha litis is the most likely diagnosis in this 10-day old infant with new onset seizures, a normal head CT scan, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing increased protein and leukocyte count with a low-norma l glucose concentration, which is consistent with aseptic (nonbacteria l) meningitis. Further suggestive is the presence of erythrocytes in the CSF which is often seen in herpetic encepha litis. Most cases of HSV encephalitis are caused by HSV-2, although infection with HSV-1 occurs and is treated in the same way. Most patients acquire the virus via transmission from the mother, often during the third trimester, with encephalitis developing usually within a week. Symptoms are nonspecific and include fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and occasiona lly seizures or focal neurologic deficits. Concomitant oral lesions may occur, but their absence does not rule out the diagnosis. The CSF findings include increased protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and a normal or low-normal glucose concentration. In many instances the causative virus can be identified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the CSF, although empiric therapy with intravenous acyclovir is warranted prior to diagnosis. Failure to recognize and treat infection can result in organ dysfunction and death, or long-term neurologic sequelae.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of increasingly frequent headac hes during the past 3 months. The headac hes are throbbing, occur only on the right side, and are associated with nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. She has had one or two headaches yearly since the age of 17 years but now has two or three week ly. She is a schoolteacher and has had no changes in work, lifestyle, or environme nt. Four months ago, conjugated estrogen therapy was begun for treatment of menopausal symptoms. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Butalbital therapy combined with acetaminophen and caffeine

correctExplanation: Migraine is a common condition that presents with recurrent primary headaches. Migraine headaches are typically severe, unilateral, throbbing, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The pain is usually located behind or adjacent to the eye. Some patients additiona lly experience an aura before or during the headache, which may present with vision loss followed by the perception of scinti llating shapes or lines and/or paresthesia. Migraine triggers include stress, menstruation and changes in hormona l concen trations , weather changes, fasting, and alcohol. Sleep may improve migraines. Patients who experience migraines associated with conjugated estrogen therapy may require discontinuation of therapy or a reduction in dose. Migraines are postulated to arise from deficient serotonin inhibition of descending pain pathways. Acute migraine treatment may include triptans and/or nonsteroidal anti­ inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For patients with disabling or frequent migraines, prophylactic treatment is also recommended and includes ~-adrenergic blockers, antidepressants such as tricycl ic antidepressants and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and anticonvulsants.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the head (Choice A) is unnecessary given a likely cause for the patient's migraines and absence of any neurologic abnormalities. Butalbital therapy combined with acetaminophen and caffeine (Choice B) may be appropriate in the treatment of a primary migraine, however, it carries risk given the adverse effects and dependency associated with barbiturates. Removal of likely offending agents is a more appropriate first step for the treatment of this patient's likely-triggered migraine. - - - - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - -- - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 1-month history of deafness, ringing in both ears, dizziness, and difficulty with balance. He also has had an occasiona l sensation that the room is spinning. He was discharged from the hospital 21 days ago after prolonged treatment for pneumon ia and sepsis with intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin. He has chronic obstruct ive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and congestive heart failure. He has a history of tubercu losis 10 years ago. Medications include digoxin, metformin, and losartan. His pulse is 84/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Examination shows nystagm us on lateral gaze bilatera lly. There is severe loss of hearing bilaterally. Air conduction is greater than bone conduct ion. Results of Weber test are normal. Muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, and sensory findings are normal. His gait is broad-based, and he is unable to walk in tandem. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ototoxicity is a frequent adverse effect of aminoglycosides, such as gentamicin, which exert bactericidal effects by binding the bacterial 30S ribosoma l subunit. Aminoglycosides accumu late in the inner ear endolymph and perilymph, and can cause cochlear ototoxicity and vestibu lotoxicity, which is typically irreversible. The risk for ototoxicity associated with aminog lycosides may be as high as 10% in some patient populations. While there is an increased risk for ototoxicity with repeat dosing or with high doses, ototoxicity may occur with even the first dose of aminog lycoside. While aminoglycosides are high ly effective against a broad range of Gram-negative bacterial infections, such as with Escherichia coli, Klebsiel/a, Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Serratia species, their use is limited by their significant adverse effects. In addition to ototoxicity and vestibulotoxicity, aminoglycosides are also associated with nephrotoxicity.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cerebel lopontine angle tumor (Choice B), such as an acoustic neuroma, meningioma, or glioma, typical ly affects the vestibulococh lear nerve and other crania l nerves (eg, trigemina l, abducens, facial nerves). Patients may present with hearing loss and vertigo; sensory and motor dysfunction of the face and/or extraocular muscles are also possible. Meniere disease (Choice C) is a condition of episodic vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss that results from pressure accumu lation in the endolymph of the inner ear. This patient's lack of episodic symptoms suggests against this diagnosis. Pontine infarction (Choice D) may occur as a seque la of basilar artery occlusion and present with trunca l ataxia, diplopia, nystagmus, locked-in state, or coma. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain in the left thigh and flank and weakness of the left leg. She has a 30-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus currently controlled with glyburide. Examination shows weakness of the left iliopsoas and quadriceps muscles. Deep tendon reflex of the left quadriceps muscle is decreased. Sensation to pinprick is decreased over the left latera l thigh and medial calf. Which of the following is the most likely location of the lesion?
correctExplanation: Lower extremity neuropathies can be caused by nerve compression, ischemia, inflammation, degeneration, infection, or transection. Diabetic patients may develop spontaneous femora l neuropathies secondary to inflammation and ischemia. The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and exits the lumbosacral plexus by passing under the inguinal ligament. Neuropathy of the femoral nerve or its roots presents with unilatera l quadriceps and iliopsoas weakness, decreased sensation over the anteromedial thigh and media l calf (the latter via its saphenous branch), and absent patellar tendon reflex.
incorrectExplanation: nd M. The axillary nerve (Choice A) arises from C5 and C6. Injury to the axillary nerve presents with weakness of shoulder abduction, as well as numbness over the deltoid region. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (Choice C) provides sensation to the antero latera l aspect of the thigh. The median nerve (Choice D) arises from C5 to T1. Injury to the median nerve causes weakness of the wrist flexors and muscles of the thenar eminence, and decreased sensation over the thenar eminence and the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ fingers. The peronea l nerve (Choice E) is a continuation of the sciatic nerve that supplies innervation to the lateral leg. Injury causes weakness of muscles within the latera l compartment of the leg. A peroneal nerve lesion also causes numbness of the posterolateral side of the leg and the dorsolateral aspect of the foot. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of visual hallucinations during the past 2 weeks. She has a 10-year history of hypertension and a 5-year history of Parkinson disease. Current medicat ions include hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, metopro lol, and carbidopa-levodo pa. Three weeks ago, her carbidopa- levodopa dose was increased because of decreased mobility, and metoprolo l was added to her medication regimen because of inadequate blood pressure contro l. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 10 years ago. She drinks one glass of wine with dinner every night. Her temperatu re is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 58/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 148/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Neurologic examination shows a resting tremor of the hands and cogwhee l rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles. Her gait is shuffling. Mental status examination shows a constr icted affect. She is oriented to person but not to place or time. She can recall one of three objects after 5 minutes. She says she sees ghost-like figures entering the room. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. A CT scan of the head shows mild atrophy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's visual hallucinations?
correctExplanation: Adverse effect of carbidopa-levodopa is the most likely cause of this patient's visual hallucinations. Parkinson disease is a progressive neurologic disease that manifests with bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, and a resting tremor. It is secondary to the destruction of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, so pharmacotherapy focuses on replacing dopamine with carbidopa-levodopa. Frequently, early in the disease course, treatment is effective, but over time, many patients experience an "on-off'' phenomenon whereby pharmacotherapy only works for a short time after each dose before the effects dissipate. This often prompts an increase in the dose of carbidopa-levodopa, or a change in the dosing interval, but in elderly patients this can result in multiple off-target adverse effects including hallucinations. This patient has no evidence of another underlying medical illness that may cause hallucinations, so the next step should be to lower the dose of carbidopa-levodopa to resolve her hallucinations. Patients who are intolerant or refractory to pharmacotherapy should be considered for deep brain stimulation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Major depressive disorder (Choice B) is diagnosed when patients meet criteria established in the DSM-5 including impaired sleep (either insomnia or hypersomnolence), loss of interest, guilt, loss of energy, poor concentration, poor appetite, psychomotor retardation , or suicidal ideation. This patient does not meet the criteria. \ j - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 5-year-o ld girl has the insidious onset of a clumsy gait over the past 3 months. Examination shows pes cavus of the left foot. There is generalized diminished girth of the left leg, and a decreased tendon reflex of the left ankle. The tendon reflexes at the knees are brisk. There is a sacral tuft of hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Tethered spinal cord, a defect in neural development whereby a caudal portion of the spinal cord becomes tethered to fixed fibrous structures that cause traction on the cord as the patient grows, is the most likely diagnosis. The filum terminale is a band of tissue that stretches between the caudal portion of the spinal cord and the sacrum, and persistent tethering of the spinal cord results in stretching as the child develops and axial growth occurs. Depending upon the severity, symptoms may present at infancy or can develop many years later, but progressive lower extremity neurologic dysfunction is typical as the spinal cord stretches and bends during normal activity. Sensory and gait abnormalities are typical, and bladder or bowel incontinence may also occur. Low back pain that worsens with activity and pain in the perineum can also occur. Clues to diagnosis include a tuft of hair over the sacrum or the presence of hemangiomas or dimples in the same region. Early detection and surgical intervention can improve symptoms and halt the progression of neurologic dysfunction.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Ataxia-telangiectasia (Choice A) is a genetic disorder that leads to early ataxia with progressively worsening gross and fine motor capabilities as children reach school age. Other findings include oculocutaneous telangiectasias and immunodeficiency. Friedreich ataxia (Choice B) is caused by a loss of function mutation in the frataxin gene resulting from a trinucleotide repeat. Patients usually present in adolescence with progressive ataxia of all limbs and dysarthria. Distal sensory loss and dysphagia may also be seen. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Choice C) has a diverse presentation but patients usually develop systemic symptoms including fevers and rash in addition to arthritis, which may affect nearly any joint. It does not present with asymmetric gait abnormalities or hyperreflexia. Spastic diplegia (Choice D) is a subtype of cerebral palsy and presents with symmetric spasticity of the lower extremities with associated sensory loss. In rare cases, the upper extremities may be involved, and intellectual disability can occur. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman with AIDS comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, slurred speech, and headache. She is right-handed. Funduscop ic examination shows papilledema . Neurologic examination shows aphasia, right homonymous hemianopia, and right-sided spastic weakness. A CT scan of the head with contrast shows multiple small ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema and mass effect in the left frontal, right occipital, and left parietal lobes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Toxop/asma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite. Transmission can occur through the ingestion of oocysts from cat feces or infected meat, direct transmission between a mother and fetus, or from organ transplantation, which leads to invasion followed by dissemination of the parasite where it typically lies dormant. It is a ubiquitous organism and nearly 10% of individua ls will be seropositive for T gondii, but the parasite does not usually cause severe disease in immunocompetent individuals. In patients with HIV infection and CD4+ T-lymphocyte counts less than 100 cells/mm 3, however, reactivation can occur with several distinct clinical syndromes of which cerebra l toxoplasmosis results in the most morbidity. Cerebral toxop lasmosis typical ly presents with multiple ring­ enhancing lesions scattered throughout the brain. Seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and systemic symptoms are common, as are signs of increased intracrania l pressure. Patients with HIV infection and positive Toxop/asma lgG antibodies are typically treated empirica lly with a sulfonamide and pyrimethamine if cerebra l toxoplasmosis is suspected, but confirmatory diagnosis occurs through a brain biopsy, which will show a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages, and plasma cells, along with the presence of the T gondii organism. Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an AIDS-defining disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cryptococcosis (Choice A) is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, an encapsulated fungus and opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients. It can cause cryptococca l meningitis, encephalitis, and pulmonary cryptococcosis. Meningoencepha litis presents subacute ly with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, often accompanied by cough and shortness of breath caused by concurrent pulmonary infection. Focal neurologic deficits and mass lesions on neuroimaging are rare. Cysticercosis (Choice B) is caused by Taenia so/ium and presents with headache, seizures, and increased intracranial pressure. Neuroimaging will show cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in the brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, and/or orbit. It less commonly presents with focal neurologic deficits such as those seen in this patient. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of progressive numbness and weakness of his legs. Six years ago, he had non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated successful ly with chemotherapy and radiation therapy. He is current ly taking no medications. Cranial nerve examination shows no abnormalities. Muscle strength is intact in the upper extremities but 3/5 in the proximal lower extremities and 4/5 in the distal lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the upper extremities and 3+ in the lower extrem ities. Babinski sign is present bilatera lly. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below the level of the nipples, and sensation to vibrat ion is decreased over the feet and ankles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Metastatic spinal cord compression occurs most commonly in prostate, lung, or breast cancer, although it can occur with any malignancy. It is generally caused by vertebral bony metastases that tend to occur in the vertebral body, particularly of the thoracic spine. Its presentation depends on the level of the lesion and the degree of spinal cord compression. Symptoms include back pain, which is often worse at night or with lying down, muscle weakness, sensory abnormalities, bladder or bowel dysfunction, and gait instability. It will general ly present with an upper motoneuron pattern of injury in the lower extremities with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski signs, as in this patient, assuming the compression is in the thoracic or upper lumbar region. Ascending numbness or paresthesias are also common. Diagnosis is classically made utilizing MRI of the spine. Patients may be treated with glucocorticoids, radiation therapy, and/or surgical decompression and spine stabilization.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chemotherapy-induced polyneuropathy (Choice A) classically presents with sensory loss and paresthesias in the distal extremities that ascend in a "stocking and glove" pattern. Most chemotherapy-induced polyneuropathy will improve over time after chemotherapy is stopped, making this a less likely explanation for this patient's acute onset of symptoms. Guillain-Barre syndrome (Choice B) is caused by autoimmune-mediated nerve destruction following a systemic infection, such as Campy/obacter jejuni. It classically presents with ascending paralysis with absent deep tendon reflexes that begins in the lower extremities. It can also ascend to involve the upper extremities, diaphragm, and crania l nerves in some patients. Myopathy (Choice D) is caused by a disorder affecting the muscle itself, rather than the nerves that innervate it. questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 62-year-o ld man has had progressive difficulty with speech and swallowing over the past year. Symptoms were subtle at first, and only he and his fam ily noticed a problem. Recent ly, two ham radio colleagues have commented that he sounds different on the air. He has also noticed that he has difficulty manipulating objects in the left hand, walking smooth ly, and going up and down stairs. He has not had any difficulty with his thought processes. Exami nation shows slow deliberate speech with mild dysarthria. Crania l nerves are otherwise norma l. There is wasting of intrinsic hand muscles and distal weakness in the left hand. Gait is slightly broad-based, but Romberg sign is absent. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the left upper extremity, 2+ in the right upper extremity, and 3+ in the lower extremities. Jaw jerk is hyperactive . His serum potassium concentrat ion is 3.2 mEq/L. An x-ray of the chest shows normal findings. Wh ich of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.G: Epidural metastatic carc inoma P) Sensorimotor periphera l neuropa thy
choices.H: Epstein-Barr virus infectio n Q) Spinal cord compression

correctExplanation: Amyotrophic latera l sclerosis (ALS) is likely given insidious onset of upper and lower motoneuron deficits. ALS is caused by the progressive destruction of motoneurons. Patients may develop asymmetric weakness of the extremities. Unilateral hand weakness, foot drop, and bulbar symptoms (eg, dysphagia, voice changes) may occur simultaneous ly. On physica l examination, the presence of both upper motoneuron signs such as hyperreflexia and spasticity, combined with lower motoneuron signs such as hyporeflexia suggests the diagnosis. Parkinsonian features such as masked facies, tremor, and shuffling gait may occur, as can autonomic dysfunction. Eventually, patients deve lop respiratory insufficiency. The clinical progression is relent less and results in death.
incorrectExplanation: , M, N, 0, P, and Q. Alcoholic rhabdomyolysis (Choice A) refers to the breakdown of muscle and the release of creatine kinase in patients who consume large quantities of alcohol. Muscle pain and renal dysfunction may occur. Becker muscu lar dystrophy (Choice C) is a myopathy presenting with muscle weakness in the absence of upper motoneuron signs. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-week history of difficulty with speech and weakness of his right leg. He has a 5-year history of HIV infection treated with antiretroviral therapy. On admiss ion, his temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows thrush. There is mild nonfluent aphasia. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the right lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the right lower extrem ity and 2+ elsewhere. Babinski sign is present on the right. An MRI of the brain shows six ring-enhancing lesions in the cerebral hemispheres bilateral ly; the largest lesion is in the left frontal lobe. Some of the lesions have surroundi ng edema. Pyrimetham ine and sulfadiazine therapy is started. Two weeks later, there is no improvement in his symptoms. A second MRI of the brain shows no decrease in the size of the lesions, and some have increased in size. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is a rare variant of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that occurs most commonly in immunocompromised patients. It can occur in the brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, or eyes. Presenting symptoms include focal neurologic deficits, vision changes, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, headache, nausea, emesis). In immunocompetent patients, neuroimaging will most commonly show a solitary, hypodense periventricular mass with well­ defined borders and mild surrounding edema. In immunocompromised patients, however, the development of primary CNS lymphoma is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, with additional risk factors in HIV including a decreased CD4+ T lymphocyte count, increased viral load, and chronic co-infection with hepatitis B or C virus. Imaging in immunocompromised patients more commonly shows multifocal disease, numerous, ring- or heterogeneously enhancing lesions throughout the corpus callosum, periventricular areas, and periependyma l regions. The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow cytometry or cytology, with evidence of EBV DNA in the CSF supporting the diagnosis. Treatment typically consists of high-dose and generally intrathecal chemotherapeutics and antiretroviral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Candida! abscesses (Choice A) of the brain can occur in immunocompromised patients. These are typically microabscesses that can lead to the development of encepha lopathy with altered mental status and are seen on MRI as small, ring-enhancing lesions often with a hemorrhagic component. However, these patients commonly present with fever, nuchal rigidity, and headache, which this patient does not demonstrate. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes fo r a routine health maintenance examination. She is concerned about developing dementia because she lives alone; she does not want to be a burden to her children. Her father was just diagnosed with dementia, Alzheimer type. She takes no medicat ions other than hydroch lorothiazide for hypertension. Her blood pressure is 124/84 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following measures is most likely to decrease her risk for multi-infarct (vascular) dementia?

choices.E: Daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation

correctExplanation: Vascular dementia is the second most common form of dementia after Alzheimer type, characterized by stepwise cognitive decline following recurrent cerebral infarctions (strokes). The rate of decline and specific symptoms depend on the regions of the brain affected, and patients typically develop cognitive impairment, motor dysfunction, and behavioral changes as the disease progresses. Risk factors include age, hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and prior cerebrovascular accidents. Diagnosis is made clinically with support of neuroimaging demonstrating cerebral ischemic changes. Risk factor reduction is the primary approach to prevention. Continued control of blood pressure is most likely to decrease the risk for this patient developing vascular dementia.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Efforts to reduce overall cardiovascular risk factors should be encouraged, which includes regular aerobic exercise (Choice B). Daily fish oil supplementation (Choice D) and daily vitamin E supplementation (Choice F) have also been shown to have a mild protective effect. However, control of blood pressure has a stronger association with cardiovascular risk reduction. Daily aspirin prophylaxis (Choice C) is recommended for patients who have existing clinically significant cardiovascular disease (such as history of a myocardial infarction or cerebrovascular event). It is not likely to significantly lower the risk for vascular dementia in this patient. Daily vitamin D and calcium supplementation (Choice E) is recommended for women who are postmenopausal, patients taking chronic systemic corticosteroids, and patients with advanced renal disease to reduce the risk for osteoporosis and fragility fractures. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 45-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after she lost consciousness while shopping in a department store; on regaining consciousness, she had a severe headache and photophobia. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examinat ion shows slight neck stiffness with flexion. There is pain with lateral deviation of the eyes. Neurologic examinat ion shows no other abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows no lesions or evidence of bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Discharg ing the patient with analgesic therapy

correctExplanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) refers to bleeding into the subarachnoid space and can be caused by aneurysmal or non-aneurysma l rupture of an artery in the subarachnoid space. Patients typically present with an acute, severe headache (often described as the worst headache of their life), along with neck stiffness, photophobia, and possible stupor or coma in severe cases. Fever can be associated with SAH and is associated with worse outcomes. CT scan of the head typically shows hyperdense blood products in the cerebral sulci and basal cisterns. However, the sensitivity of CT scan for SAH is lower with small volume bleeding or a delayed presentation. If there is strong suspicion for SAH with a negative CT scan, a lumbar puncture can be performed, which may show red blood cells or xanthochromia, which represents hemoglobin degradation products. As the blood products circulate within the subarachnoid space, complications include the development of communicating and/or obstructive hydrocephalus in the acute stage, along with the potential for re-bleeding and vasospasm in the days following the initial bleed. It is a neurosurgical emergency that may be fatal if progressive or untreated.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Admission for observation (Choice A) would not be indicated until further workup is performed to evaluate for subarachnoid hemorrhage. First, a subarachnoid hemorrhage should be investigated by lumbar puncture, and if findings are consistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage, vessel imaging should occur to evaluate for aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. Discharging the patient with analgesic therapy (Choice B) would be dangerous in the care of this patient, as further evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage is indicated. The patient is at risk for hydrocephalus, vasospasm, rebleeding, or severe hemorrhage after a sentinel bleed. - - - ------ --- -- -- - -- -- --- - -- - - - -- - - -- --- - -- - - -- -- - - - - -- - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman with alcoholism is hospitalized for detoxification. On the second day after admission, she has an impaired sensor ium and a decreased attention span during examination. She appears frightened and disoriented and shrieks, "Make the snakes go away." Her temperatu re is 38.3°C (101 °F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 190/120 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient has developed delirium tremens, a serious complication of alcoho l withdrawal. Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol results in imbalanced and unopposed sympathetic excess. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can begin within hours after the cessation of alcohol use. Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, involves severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visua l hallucinations, and autonomic instability (generally characterized by tachycardia, hypertension, and potentially hyperthermia). As in this patient, delirium tremens can begin 2 to 5 days after the patient's last alcoho lic drink. Delirium tremens is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (GABA A receptor agonists) to address the psychomotor agitation associated with withdrawal and prevent the worsening of withdrawa l manifestations. The specific benzodiazepines utilized include chlordiazepoxide, a long-acting benzodiazepine given on a scheduled basis in patients experiencing or at risk for complicated withdrawal (eg, delirium tremens), and/or lorazepam, a short-acting benzodiazepine given as-needed for withdrawal symptoms. Management also includes frequent assessments including vital sign checks, fluid resuscitation, and nutritiona l supplementation (especial ly with commonly deficient vitamins and minerals such as thiamine, potassium, and magnesium).

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe low back pain and severe shooting pain down her left buttock and leg. The pain began when she arose quickly from a seated position to open a sliding glass door. Two analgesic tablets leftover from a dental procedure provided no relief. She is an avid cyclist. On arrival, intravenous administration of morphine is begun and provides minimal relief. The patient notes numbness over the perineum when she attempts to void. She is reluctant to move from a flexed, seated position to a stretcher because of the pain. Muscle strength is 3/5 on great toe extension, dorsiflexion, and plantar flexion of the left foot. Knee jerk is present on the left. Achilles tendon reflex is absent on the left. An MRI of the lumbosacra l spine shows a large central herniation at L4-5 that compresses the L5 and S1 nerves on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome occurs as a result of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs because of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidura l or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void and urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy , can help control pain, and may transiently improve neurologic function secondary to decreasing edema at the site of cord compression. However, cauda equina syndrome is a surgica l emergency and requires decompression with lumbar laminectomy as soon as possible.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. A bone scan (Choice A) is used to examine and diagnose abnormalities in bones, such as bony metastases, fractures, or osteomyelitis. It is not used to evaluate neuromuscular weakness. Physical therapy (Choice B) can be used in the management of other types of back pain, such as lumbosacral strain. However, lumbosacra l strain will not cause perinea! anesthesia or neuromuscular weakness. Cauda equina is a surgical emergency, making physical therapy an incorrect initial next step. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man comes to the physician 2 hours after the onset of dizz iness, nausea, and unsteadi ness . He had a whiplash neck inju ry 2 years ago and is still receiving monthly chiropractic man ipulations. His voice is hoarse . There is left ptosis and nystagmus . The left pupil is 2 mm smaller than the right. There is decreased sensation to pain over the left side of the face and right extrem ities. He has atax ia on the left. Mental status exam ination shows no abnorma lities. Wh ich of the following arteries is most likely to be occluded?

correctExplanation: This patient likely has an occlusion of the left vertebra l artery leading to vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Vertebrobasi lar insufficiency can be caused by ischemia in patients with poor sympathetic regulation or thromboembolism common ly originating from an atherosclerotic plaque in or dissection of the vertebra l artery (known as a posterior circulation stroke). A thrombus of the vertebral artery commonly forms from atherosclerotic disease but may also form as a result of an intima l defect from trauma or vertebra l artery dissection, a known complication of chiropractic manipu lation. The brain stem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes are common ly affected. Patients typica lly present with vestibu locerebe llar signs (eg, ataxia, dysmetria, dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vomiting, nystagmus), ipsilatera l cranial nerve dysfunction (eg, dysphagia, dysarthria, vertical or horizonta l gaze palsies), contralateral hemiparesis (caused by corticospinal tract damage), contralateral impairment in pain and temperature sensation (caused by spinothalamic tract damage), and/or contra latera l homonymous hemianopsia with macu lar sparing (caused by posterior cerebral artery involvement). In posterior circulation strokes affecting the lateral pons, Horner syndrome may occur, which presents with unilateral ptosis and miosis (pupil lary constriction) and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis. If no hemorrhage is shown on noncontrast CT scan of the head, acute management of posterior circu lation strokes may involve tissue plasminogen activator therapy or thrombectomy. In dissection, antiplatelet and anticoagu lant administration is indicated to prevent conversion to a thromboembolic stroke if none has yet occurred.

Compared to vertebral artery occlusion, basilar artery occlusion may present with more acute and severe corticospina l and corticobu lbar dysfunction, leading to locked-in syndrome. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the phys ician because of a 4-month history of headac hes and blurred vision. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medicat ions. Menses occur at irregular 2- to 10-week intervals . She has had an 18-kg (40-lb) weight gain during the past 7 months. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and now weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Her tem perature is 37°C (98.6 °F). Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Visua l field testing shows no abnorma lities. Funduscop ic examination shows blurred optic discs; there are no spontaneous venous pulsations. The rema inder of the exam ination shows no abnormalities. A CT scan of the head shows small lateral ventricles. On lumbar puncture, the opening pressure is 290 mm H 20; cerebrospina l fluid (CSF) analysis shows no leukocytes or erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
correctExplanation: Impaired resorption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is the primary mechanism behind pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). IIH is characterized by signs of increased intracranial pressure including headache, papilledema, and increased opening pressure on lumbar puncture without any underlying pathology to cause such findings on neuroimaging. It is primari ly seen in young women who are overweight. Although there is no malignant cause underlying the increased intracranial pressure, it may cause debilitating headaches and permanent vision loss. Headaches that are secondary to increased intracranial pressure often are worse when lying down and relieved by standing. The most common risk factors for the development of pseudotumor cerebri include female gender and obesity. However, hypervitaminosis A from increased dietary intake is another potentia l cause of IIH. This can be from excessive dietary intake or from the use of retinoid medications such as isotretinoin or all-trans retinoic acid. Other medications associated with IIH include tetracyclines, danazo l, and growth hormone.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aqueductal stenosis (Choice A) causes dilation of the lateral and third ventricles and is a cause of hydrocephalus in children. Idiopathic increased intracranial pressure presents with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (nausea, vomiting, positiona l headache) without hydrocepha lus. Cerebel lar astrocytoma (Choice B) is a primary centra l nervous system tumor seen most often in children and a potential cause of secondary intracranial hypertension and hydrocepha lus if it obstructs the flow of CSF. IIH is characterized by increased intracranial pressure but not hydrocephalus. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a ?-month history of progressive bilateral leg pain. She describes bilateral buttock, posterior thigh, and calf pain that begins after standing or walking for 10 minutes. It is relieved in 2 minutes by bending forward at the waist or sitting. She has coronary artery disease and underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 2 years ago. Neurologic examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Doppler flow studies of the lower extremities

correctExplanation: The patient is presenting with symptoms suggestive of spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Spinal stenosis describes narrowing of the central canal, neural foramen, or lateral recesses of the spine with subsequent nerve compression and ischemia. Common causes include degenerative arthritis, spondyloarthropathies, degenerative disc disease, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and osteophyte formation in the facet joints. Neurogenic claudication describes low back pain with radiation to the buttocks and lower extremities that results from increased nerve compression, as may occur with extension of the spine during standing and walking downhill. Reducing narrowing within the spinal column with spinal flexion as during sitting or walking uphill tends to relieve the pain. Diagnostic evaluation involves x-ray imaging followed by MRI of the lumbar spine.

Carotid duplex ultrasonography (Choice A) is recommended to screen for atherosclerotic plaque in patients with a known cardiovascular disease history or significant risk factors. If a stroke or transient ischemic attack were suspected as the cause of the patient's neurologic symptoms, carotid duplex ultrasonography should be performed to evaluate for intervenab le lesions. The exacerbating and alleviating factors in this case are more suggestive of spinal stenosis. Doppler flow studies of the lower extremities (Choice B) are useful in distinguishing neurogenic claudication from claudication caused by peripheral vascu lar disease. Vascular claudication is typically relieved by rest as opposed to postura l changes. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (Choice C) can be used to confirm the presence of radiculopathy caused by nerve root compression or evaluate for other myopathy or neuropathy as the cause of the patient's symptoms. Fifteen years ago, she underwent a left radical mastectomy followed by radiation therapy of the chest wall for breast cancer. There has been no evidence of recurrence of breast cancer.
